title: Remembrance
hook: poppies, silence, and prayers for all who died in war

segments.voice: Yesterday, All Souls: candles lit and graves visited for the faithful departed. Your line was rest eternal. Whose name did you hold in the light? Day one thousand fifty-seven.

A red paper flower, pinned to a coat. Then another, on a bus driver. Another on a newsreader. In some countries, poppies like these bloom on coats each autumn, and then, on one morning, a whole street goes quiet. Traffic stops. A shop falls silent mid-sale. At a stone memorial, someone reads a poem, and the crowd answers it with a few plain words: we will remember them. Churches keep this day too. Prayers are said for all who died in war, soldiers and civilians, names known and names lost. It's a morning when the church brings its own words to a nation's silence. Today's word: Remembrance.

Start with the flower. An old war poem, In Flanders Fields, sees poppies blowing between rows of crosses over the graves of the dead. The red poppy people wear grew, so the usual account goes, out of that picture. It isn't a Bible symbol. But the church found it already had words for this day. First, silence. Ecclesiastes has a whole poem of times and seasons, and in the middle of it, in the King James words: "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak." At Remembrance, the silence comes first, before any speech or name. Second, love. On the night before he died, Jesus told his friends: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Some memorials carry that line, cut into stone. Many Christians hear it first about Jesus himself, and then about anyone who gave their life for someone else. Third, hope. Remembrance is not a celebration of war. The prophet Isaiah saw a day when the nations "shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." Some churches read that line at Remembrance, and pray for the dead of every side. Christians disagree about war. Some churches accept that a nation may fight to defend the weak; others refuse to bear arms at all, and keep this day with their whole weight on peace. Both can stand in the same silence. And for many Christians, that silence isn't empty. It's a kind of prayer: holding the dead before God, and asking for fewer names to read next time.

Here's the practice: keep two minutes' silence. The bell will hold just that. Stand if you can, or sit very still. Bring to mind one person who died in a war: a face in an old family photo, a name on a memorial you pass, someone from the news. If no name comes, hold the ones nobody remembers. Don't fill the silence with thinking. Let it be heavy. If you pray, you can hold them before God, with Isaiah's hope: neither shall they learn war any more. If you don't, just stand with them. The bell holds the time.
Remembrance. Standing still together for all who died in war, with poppies, silence, and prayer for peace.
Your line: we will remember. Today, find one name on a war memorial, a plaque, or in your family's story, and read it slowly, once, all the way through. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

howItsDone: In some countries, churches hold Remembrance services with poppies, a two-minute silence at a memorial, names of the dead read aloud, and prayers for peace and for all who died in war.

notes: Claims rule: no date (11 November, the eleventh hour, 1918) or war is named; 'a few weeks each autumn' and 'one morning' are kept vague on purpose. Confirm whether the Keeper wants the date added with a source.

'we will remember them' is the closing line of Binyon's 'For the Fallen' (1914, public domain in the US) as said at services; it is given without quotation marks and cited as a paraphrase because Binyon is not on the validator's translation list. Confirm.
The origin of the remembrance poppy in McCrae's 'In Flanders Fields' is attributed ('so the usual account goes'). Confirm.
'Some memorials carry that line' (John 15:13) and 'some churches read' Isaiah 2:4 at Remembrance are general observations, not from the cited text; soften or cut if preferred.

Differing Christian views on war are described without naming churches (just-war acceptance vs. peace churches that refuse to bear arms). Confirm fairness; consider naming Mennonites, Quakers and Brethren if the Keeper prefers.
'On the night before he died' places John 15 within the farewell discourse at the last supper (John 13–17). Confirm.
Original: זָכַר (zakhar), to remember; the note's 'can be something you do' is an interpretive summary. Confirm.

Editor pass: 'a poem from that war' (no war had been named) became 'an old war poem'; 'a few weeks' cut from the hook; the myth reveal now attributes the poppy origin; 'often' in the original note softened; carry changed from saying a name aloud (repeated 1055–1056) to reading one name on a memorial.
Second editor pass: the first myth reveal, which read awkwardly ('so the usual account goes, it comes from'), now says the usual account traces the poppy to In Flanders Fields.

Audit pass: narrator's 'No speech could carry what the silence carries' (an assertion) cut; 'Christians read it first about Jesus' and 'for a Christian, that silence isn't empty' softened to 'many Christians'. Practice (bring to mind one person who died) sits close to day 1056's candle practice; kept because the index sets the two-minute silence, but the Keeper may want it varied.
